The '''{{lang|nl|Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica}}''' (abbr. '''CWI'''; English: "National Research Institute for Mathematics and Computer Science") is a research centre in the field of [[mathematics]] and  [[theoretical computer science]]. It is part of the institutes organization of the [[Dutch Research Council]] (NWO) and is located at the [[Amsterdam Science Park]]. This institute is famous as the creation site of the programming language [[Python (programming language)|Python]]. It was a founding member of the European Research Consortium for Informatics and Mathematics (ERCIM).

==Early history==
The institute was founded in 1946 by [[Johannes van der Corput]], [[David van Dantzig]], [[Jurjen Koksma]], [[Hendrik Anthony Kramers]], [[Marcel Minnaert]] and [[Jan Arnoldus Schouten]]. It was originally called ''Mathematical Centre'' (in Dutch: ''Mathematisch Centrum''). One early mission was to develop mathematical prediction models to assist large Dutch engineering projects, such as the  [[Delta Works]]. During this early period, the Mathematics Institute also helped with designing the wings of the [[Fokker F27 Friendship]] airplane, voted in 2006 as the most beautiful Dutch design of the 20th century.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cwi.nl/news/2006/Fokker-F27-Friendship-wins-2006-Best-Dutch-Design-Election|title=Fokker F27 Friendship wins 2006 Best Dutch Design Election}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.trouw.nl/nieuws/fokker-friendship-beste-nederlandse-design~b73b62f7/|title = Fokker Friendship beste Nederlandse design|date = 5 May 2006}}</ref>

The computer science component developed soon after. [[Adriaan van Wijngaarden]], considered the founder of computer science (or ''informatica'') in the Netherlands, was the director of the institute for almost 20 years. [[Edsger Dijkstra]] did most of his early influential work on algorithms and formal methods at CWI. The first Dutch computers, the [[Electrologica X1]] and [[Electrologica X8]], were both designed at the centre, and [[Electrologica]] was created as a spinoff to manufacture the machines.

In 1983, the name of the institute was changed to Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) to reflect a governmental push for emphasizing computer science research in the Netherlands.<ref>Bennie Mols: ''ERCOM: The Centrum voor Wiskunde en Informatica turns 60.'' In: Newsletter of the European Mathematical Society, No. 56 (September 2007), p. 43 ([https://www.ems-ph.org/journals/newsletter/pdf/2007-09-65.pdf online])</ref>

==Recent research==
The institute is known for its work in fields such as [[operations research]], [[software engineering]], information processing, and mathematical applications in [[life sciences]] and [[logistics]].
More recent examples of research results from CWI include the development of scheduling algorithms for the Dutch railway system (the [[Nederlandse Spoorwegen]], one of the busiest rail networks in the world) and the development of the [[Python (programming language)|Python programming language]] by [[Guido van Rossum]]. Python has played an important role in the development of the [[Google search]] platform from the beginning, and it continues to do so as the system grows and evolves.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://python.org/about/quotes/ |title=Quotes about Python |publisher=Python.org |access-date=2012-07-13}}</ref> 
Many information retrieval techniques used by packages such as [[SPSS]] were initially developed by Data Distilleries, a CWI [[Corporate spin-off|spinoff]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bloorresearch.com/analysis/spss-and-data-distilleries/ |title=SPSS and Data Distilleries |publisher=Python.org |access-date=2015-02-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150224133541/http://www.bloorresearch.com/analysis/spss-and-data-distilleries/ |archive-date=2015-02-24 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Sumath |last2=Sivanandam |first1=S |first2=S.N. |date=2006 |title=Introduction to Data Mining and its Applications
 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |page=743 |isbn=978-3-540-34350-9 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-34351-6 }}</ref>

Work at the institute was recognized by national or international research awards, such as the [[Lanchester Prize]] (awarded yearly by [[INFORMS]]), the [[Gödel Prize]] (awarded by [[ACM SIGACT]]) and the [[Spinoza Prize]]. Most of its senior researchers hold part-time professorships at other Dutch universities, with the institute producing over 170 full professors during the course of its history. Several CWI researchers have been recognized as members of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]], the [[Academia Europaea]], or as knights in the [[Order of the Netherlands Lion]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cwi.nl/news/2013/cwi-lectures-organized-in-honour-of-mathematician-lex-schrijver |title=Lex Schrijver receives EURO Gold Medal 2015 |publisher=cwi |date=2013-04-25 |access-date=2018-02-19}}</ref>

In February 2017, CWI in association with [[Google]] announced a successful [[collision attack]] on [[SHA 1]] encryption algorithm.<ref>[https://security.googleblog.com/2017/02/announcing-first-sha1-collision.html Announcing the first SHA1 collision]</ref>

==Early European Internet==
{{Further|Internet in the Netherlands}}
CWI was a pioneer of the [[Internet]] in Europe through the implementation of a [[Internet protocol suite|TCP/IP]] connection to [[National Science Foundation Network|NSFNET]] in 1988.<ref>{{Cite web |title=CWI Celebrates 30 Years of Open Internet in Europe |url=https://ercim-news.ercim.eu/en115/ib/cwi-celebrates-30-years-of-open-internet-in-europe |access-date=2026-08-23 |website=ercim-news.ercim.eu}}</ref>{{Refn|The UK and Norway had been connected to the [[ARPANET]] since 1973 and Norway and [[University College London]] (UCL) adopted TCP/IP in 1982, ahead of the ARPANET.|group=nb}} [[Piet Beertema]] at CWI established the first sustained connection outside the United States to the NSFNET for [[EUnet]] on 17 November 1988.<ref name="cwi-history" />{{Refn|This was shortly after France's [[French Institute for Research in Computer Science and Automation|INRIA]] achieved a connection to the NSFNET.<ref name=":0">{{cite book|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TzslDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA84|title=The Routledge Companion to Global Internet Histories|date=2017|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=978-1317607656|pages=84–89|chapter=The path to digital literacy and network culture in France (1980s to 1990s)}}</ref><ref>[''Et Dieu crea l'Internet'', Christian Huitema, {{ISBN|2-212-08855-8}}, 1995, page 10]</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://thetechnologytrend.blogspot.com/2012/03/brief-history-of-internet.html|title=A brief history of the internet|last=Andrianarisoa|first=Menjanirina|date=2 March 2012}}</ref>|group=nb}}

The first Dutch [[country code top-level domain]] (ccTLD) issued was cwi.nl.<ref name="cwi-history">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cwi.nl/about/history/cwi-achievements-details|title=CWI History: details|website=CWI|language=en-gb|access-date=2020-02-09}}</ref><ref>{{in lang|nl}} [https://www.sidn.nl/over-sidn/geschiedenis/ De geschiedenis van SIDN] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130727033624/https://www.sidn.nl/over-sidn/geschiedenis/ |date=2013-07-27 }} (History of SIDN), [http://www.sidn.nl Official website] of SIDN</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.internethalloffame.org/blog/2016/09/09/kees-neggers-global-networking-requires-global-collaboration|title=Kees Neggers: Global Networking Requires Global Collaboration {{!}} Internet Hall of Fame|website=www.internethalloffame.org|date=9 September 2016 |access-date=2020-04-03}}</ref> When this domain was registered on 1 May 1986, [[.nl]] became the first active ccTLD outside the [[United States]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.sidn.nl/en/about-sidn/our-milestones |title=Our milestones |website=SIDN |access-date=2022-08-17 |archive-date=2020-08-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200808001755/https://www.sidn.nl/en/about-sidn/our-milestones |url-status=dead }}</ref>{{Refn|The [[.uk]] ccTLD was registered in July 1985, seven months after the original [[generic top-level domain]]s such as [[.com]] and the first country code after [[.us]].|group=nb}} For the first ten years CWI, or rather Beertema, managed the .nl administration, until in 1996 this task was transferred to its spin-off SIDN.<ref name="cwi-history" />

The [[Amsterdam Internet Exchange]] (one of the largest Internet Exchanges in the world, in terms of both members and throughput traffic) is located at the neighbouring [[Stichting Academisch Rekencentrum Amsterdam|SARA]] (an early CWI spin-off) and [[Nikhef]] institutes. The [[World Wide Web Consortium]] (W3C) office for the Benelux countries is located at CWI.<ref>{{cite web |title=The World Wide Web Consortium - Benelux Office |url=https://www.w3c.nl/contact |access-date=2022-08-17 |publisher=W3C}}</ref>

==Spin-off companies==
CWI has demonstrated a continuing effort to put the work of its researchers at the disposal of society, mainly by collaborating with commercial companies and creating spin-off businesses. In 2000 CWI established "CWI Incubator BV", a dedicated company with the aim to generate high tech spin-off companies.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cwi.nl/general/spinoff-companies |title=Spin-off companies' details |publisher=CWI Amsterdam |access-date=2014-07-08 |archive-date=14 July 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714204515/https://www.cwi.nl/general/spinoff-companies |url-status=dead }}</ref> Some of the CWI spinoffs include:<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cwi.nl/sharing-knowledge/spin-offs |title=Spin-off companies |publisher=CWI Amsterdam |access-date=2014-07-08 |archive-date=3 July 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140703234853/http://www.cwi.nl/sharing-knowledge/spin-offs |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* 1956: [[Electrologica]], a pioneering Dutch computer manufacturer.
* 1971: [[Stichting Academisch Rekencentrum Amsterdam|SARA]] (now called [[SURFnet|SURF]]), founded as a center for data processing activities for [[Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam]], [[Universiteit van Amsterdam]], and the CWI.
* 1990: [[DigiCash]], an electronic money corporation founded by [[David Chaum]].
* 1994: [[NLnet Foundation|NLnet]], an [[Internet service provider]].
* 1994: General Design / Satama Amsterdam, a design company, acquired by [[LBi]] (then Lost Boys international).
* 1995: Data Distilleries, developer of analytical database software aimed at information retrieval, eventually becoming part of [[SPSS]] and acquired by [[IBM]].
* 1996: [https://sidn.nl Stichting Internet Domeinregistratie Nederland (SIDN)], the [[.nl]] top-level [[domain registrar]].
* 2000: [https://www.softwareimprovementgroup.com Software Improvement Group (SIG)], a software improvement and legacy code analysis company.
* 2008: [[MonetDB]], a high-tech database technology company, developer of the MonetDB [[Column-oriented DBMS|column-store]].
* 2008: [[Vectorwise]], an analytical database technology company, founded in cooperation with the  [[Ingres Corporation]] (now [[Actian]]) and eventually acquired by it.
* 2010: [http://www.spinque.com Spinque], a company providing search technology for information retrieval specialists.
* 2013: [https://monetdbsolutions.com MonetDB Solutions], a database services company.
* 2016: [http://seita.nl Seita], a technology company providing demand response services for the energy sector.
* 2021: [https://duckdblabs.com DuckDB Labs],  a data processing company offering support and consulting services for DuckDB (a column-oriented RDBMS, designed for high performance on complex queries against large databases in embedded configurations).
